title: What are we to make of the hypereroticized decor of the places Alex breaks into in Clockwork Orange?

commenti.body: I see it as satire and a comment on bourgeoisie middle class lifestyles. It shows that even the supposed good people are drowning in the excess and hedonism that Alex and his droogs delight in.

where does eroticism cross the line and become hedonism? 

Also I wouldn't consider the cat lady and Frank representative of middle class lifestyles. That aside, they also don't appear to be excessively hedonistic. Idiosyncratic, sure, in both behavior and aesthetic taste. But it's unclear they exhibit any moral depravity that should be spoken of in the same breath as Alex's

To me Kubrick’s films are a reflection of society as he sees it, so I see in ACO the juxtaposition of Alex and his hedonistic violence and grittiness with the bourgeoisie socialites who try to control him, who are represented as innocent with a hidden agenda. To me it’s a pretty clear social commentary, the entire film is exactly that.

agreed in broad strokes but I think that misses some of the nuance with the cat lady and frank. They seem to be minding their own business when Alex enters their lives. They're not trying to control him at all. Eventually they do seek revenge on him, but that comes from a place of revenge rather than control

Yeah nuance like Alex crushing her with a giant pottery penis. Very nuanced. 

I think it’s pretty obvious what we are meant to take from that scene.
but if they're just trying to control him it would be overkill to torture him by playing Beethoven's 9th

Which is why they aren’t just controlling him, they are living out their own fantasies and desires of violence and sadism. 

Are you starting to see the point yet?
I see what you're saying but I don't see why you'd favor that explanation vs. a pure revenge motive. The dude's wife was raped. Seeking revenge isn't exactly sadistic in that case, no?

Well yeah but that’s just surface level, we are talking about social commentary and messages derived from the film. 

It is apples and a clockwork oranges
yah I can see your case for repressed violent tendencies. Just trying to square that with Alex's POV though

I don’t think we should judge them. Rich people can keep lots of stuff. A sex pest can be a sex pest. A rapist. A gross human being. It’s not inherently wrong to keep weird sex stuff. It is thought to use it in a rape. That’s why the character is so scary. You think it’s safe to keep sex related things around the house, well guess what. As a device in film, it’s meant to shame the victims. Make them feel like it’s partially their fault for being dirty sinners already. Like they deserved the actions that happened next.
POV in what sense, as in regarding the actual story or possible symbolism?

Critic Roger Ebert was offended by the film. He thought Kubrick glorified Alex and pointed to the use of the fish eye lens to make the audience see the world as distorted from the perspective of Alex. Unlike the novel's original ending where Alex grows up and reflects that he's not so young after all, the film omits this ending and ends on a more ominous note. 

The treatment facility is a sterile and orderly, which brings to mind fascist values. This starkly contrasts with the hedonistic decor of assumably the conservative cat woman's and the liberal Frank Alexander's home. It brings to mind Epstein, who possibly helped Trump and Bill Clinton have affairs with young women. 

There are antinomian puritans who preach against sin, but whose personal lives are definitely not straightlaced. Take for example the current US speaker of the house that some believe may be an ex-gay. He and his son monitor each other's internet activities. He characterized being gay as a dark harbinger of chaos and sexual anarchy. If he is an ex gay, then his self denial is pathological.

Alex is like this guy's opposite: he's all id. He doesn't have sufficient conscience to stop him from doing actually evil things. I never read Brave New World, but Huxley was arguably correct when he surmised fascism would thrive from positive reinforcement than negative reinforcement like in 1984. Like in the movie Parasite, perhaps there's the suggestion that the insulated upper class aren't just hedonistic like Alex, but their hands aren't clean either. Because the rules for the wealthy aren't the same as the rules for the rest of us.

I read a short story about a Communist utopia where people escaped into the world of sex at home, where they could truly be free. Free from the suppression of their government but also free from the world's troubles. But this is also true for capitalism. In the documentary The Century of Self, the filmmaker explores how the media helped shape a cult of consumerism and individualism. He also argued elsewhere about oh dearism; like in Putin's Russia, elites benefit from the public feeling that truth is unknowable; then people just want the safety of their home where things are safe and they're their own master. It's no coincidence that in Islamist countries, women are treated like male property.

Good catch. 

Didn't Kubrick outright address it in that interview? It was one of the few (if not only) times he outright said what a movie is about. 

IIRC he said something along the lines of the elites of the country influenced society to become hyper obsessed with sex and pop culture. The elites wanted to set up a fascistic dictatorship while the population is distractedly obsessing over meaningless things. That is why they created the (possibly fake) treatment to empty out the prisons. During his tour of the prison the politician says something along the lines of needing the newly freed space for political dissidents.

It's intended to show the society in which he grew up. We are kinda given an explanation through those locations that Alex is a product of this society. One thing that Kubrick does throughout the movie is not blame Alex. He is never the problem, it is the society and the people around him. 
Kubrick removes the blame from Alex, which helps in the second half as the same society wants him to change. And when he changes he isn't being accepted.  This is Kubrick's way of make you empathize with Alex. I am not sure if the intention was to make us empathize, Iam completely missing it there ig

> where does eroticism cross the line and become hedonism? 

I would say at the point where things become less fully focused on sex, and the intent is more focused on pleasure versus exposing the human body in an artistic fashion.
I'm intrigued by this short story. Do you remember what it was?
Now that I think about it, I'm not sure if it was a short story. Maybe I'm misremembering and it was some essay or something.

The film is easier to understand if you see it as a failed satire, but a successful black comedy. The satirical details, such as the one you listed, never come together to form a coherent critique, which a satire must have. The only competent satire is when Alex receives his treatment, but it's not very cutting - it darkly mocks the idea that criminals can be saved; that a belief in free will and goodness can be instilled in such people. McDowell's performance is what makes it a great movie; Kubrick just made it nice to look at and listen to.

The question you’re asking is a good one, and there is no clear answer to it - the movie seeks to explore that. Just like critics of ACO might call it pornographic or perhaps even “torture porn”, one could look at the cat lady and her erotic art and call her a consumer of pornography. Is it porn though? Unclear, but what is clear is that what she’s doing is turning people into objects - naked women in her paintings, or the penis sculpture. Is that inherently a bad thing? Maybe not, but when we see women objectified as footstool statues in the bar, we understand THAT is bad. So what is the functional difference between that and reducing a man to a penis sculpture you can own and use as you please? 

It shows that while what Alex does is reprehensible,  regular members of society engage in similar behaviors. It shows that although Alex takes things to an extreme, it’s unclear what is nature vs taught by his environment. And that ties into the ideas of justice, rehabilitation, and who gets to judge others. When Alex enters prison he is stripped and basically sexually assaulted in a way that’s almost mandated by the state. What is the functional difference between that and the way abuses others? If that is what the good guys with authority are doing what does it say about as a society when we choose to condemn only Alex? 

Movie explores lots of deep human questions with no clear answers. That is why it will never feel dated

There’s generally a practical justification for each of these examples, rather than a purely intellectual one.

>The Korova Milk Bar: Filled with furniture shaped like naked female figures. The tables and chairs have mannequin-like forms that are used by patrons to drink milk-plus, a drug-laced drink.

In the late 60s/early 70s milk bars in the UK were where teenagers and scenesters genuinely hung out. The hyper-sexualization of the décor is to show that hyper-sexualization itself is a big part of the youth culture as it exists within the film. The ornate, sexism of the furnishings would genuinely appeal to kids like Alex and his Droogs and be seen as a cool place that reflect their own sensibilities (the fashionable mixed with the profane.)

>Cat Woman's House: Scene literally opens with the cat lady's crotch. House filled with erotic art, including a large statue of a phallus, which Alex later uses as a weapon.

The Cat Lady’s house is a health club, so the kinetic phallus is a physical reminder of the human body and its actions. The pop art depictions of female physicality contrasts against this and gives us an (the scene also includes exercise equipment – another link to the physical.)

That the art is ubiquitous throughout the film is a potential sign that what was at the time counter cultural was, in the not-too-distant future of the film’s setting, now comfortably installed within the mainstream, showing how the permissive attitudes of the 1960s and early 70s had become more permissive with time.

That the scene opens with a crotch shot is more to do with Kubrick’s voyeurism and objectification of his characters than a part of the film’s commentary on permissiveness. See also the gratuitous and performative nudity during the rape scenes, or the nurse being introduced with her breasts spilling out of her uniform.

>Alex's Bedroom: Alex's own bedroom is adorned with explicit imagery. His wallpaper is patterned with repeated phallic symbols, and there are paintings and photographs of naked women on the wall.

Alex is a teenager and as such hypersexual by inclination. His main interests are classical music, kitsch art, violent suffering and sex, and all these things are reflected in his bedroom.

>Ludovico Medical Facility: Although not "oversexualized" in a traditional sense, the Ludovico treatment facility where Alex undergoes his aversion therapy is filled with exaggerated, stark clinical décor.

This is just what hospitals and universities in the UK looked like in the 1970s. Kubrick did very little in terms of production design here. These places were stark and clinical because 1) Brutalism had been a major design choice in British architecture beginning in the 1960s and 2) our healthcare system is publicly funded, not privately funded, and as such didn’t historically lend itself to more decorative environments.

>Frank Alexander's Home: The home of the writer Alex later victimizes is designed with avant-garde and provocative artwork.

Frank is a writer of “subversive literature” who lives with his fashionable wife. The décor of the house simply reflects their bohemian sensibilities.

Really, to understand a lot of this you have to understand the politics of the book and the politics of Britain at the time the book was written.

The book isn’t simply about free will, it’s about state control. It’s about how the establishment, represented by the government, the police, the doctors and the prison system, weaponize permissiveness against itself in order to maintain control of the system.

In the 1960s, Britain was becoming a much more progressive society. Burgess’s book accurately predicts that if the culture continued to become more permissive and more progressive in its attitudes and outlook that the government (which upholds the Conservative values of the establishment) would eventually have to find a way to turn back the clock. They do this by creating poverty, which leads to crime, which necessitates law and order, as we see in the book/film.

At the end of the film, Alex is cured of his deprograming, but is now used as a pawn to rehabilitate the conservative government that tortured him, and in turn used as a weapon against the progressive left-wing element that tried to bring his suffering to light. So, the victimizer becomes the victim and the real victim is painted a deranged crank with dangerous ideas.

The establishment wins.

The future that Kubrick depicts is simply the reality of late 1960s Britian exaggerated by a few years. All of the art we see in the film is art specific to the period. But rather than being counter cultural, as it was at the time of the production, it’s become (in the film’s imagined future) a part of the mainstream. This illustrates the permissiveness of the culture as it exists, in contrasts with the poverty and authoritarianism that conservative governments enforce upon their people, which in turn leads to Alex’s criminality.

> It shows that even the supposed good people are drowning in the excess and hedonism that Alex and his droogs delight in.

With respect, this is a VERY conservative take. There's a huge difference between owning a work of genuine modern art and being a thief and a rapist.

>I see in ACO the juxtaposition of Alex and his hedonistic violence and grittiness with the bourgeoisie socialites who try to control him

The Cat Lady is an innocent victim who doesn't even know who Alex is. Frank Alexander is a part of a 'subversive' left-wing political group opposed to what the government is doing. Neither is trying to control him (though Frank and his collaborators are trying to use him for their own purposes - i.e. to destroy the government.)

The only people trying to control Alex are represented by every branch of the government.

The society depicted in ACO is hardly bourgeoisie - it's merely an exaggeration of the actual Britain of the late 60s and early 70s. In other words, an explosion of permissive youth culture set against a grey urban sprawl of poverty and criminality.

Would Kubrick have made “sex bladerunner” sets if he has the production budget for it? We can’t know, but we do know he deliberately crafted a leaner film shot on location. A response to 2001 burnout.

The hyper-erotic decor combined with the sheer tackiness of almost everything (except for Alex' mostly fine taste in things which is a stark contrast), speaks to me of the state of the culture portrayed, and adds depth to Alex's character with respect to just what spawned him and what he is rebelling against.  Does it suggest some grand conceit?  Not sure.  Maybe the oversexualized culture represents the womb of our "protagonist."  


I kind of thought showing such things in the movie was done because it could be done for the first time in a mainstream film in 1970, and it's not much more complex than that, save for perhaps an oddly paradoxical, self-referential moralizing comment on where such things being on public display will get us.
